judgments.reasoning_cat1: The grant is largely standard, but "approximately 10.89 acres" and the catch-all "any and all rights, privileges, easements and appurtenances, if any, thereunto belonging" leave the boundary of what passes somewhat open. The bed-of-street clause conveying to the center line of streets "opened or proposed" is the kind of general language whose reach can be argued.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits against Section 3, which requires a deed with "new legal descriptions" reflecting the City's plat of vacation of Sixth and Abbott Streets, and against the attachment list showing Exhibit A carries two legal descriptions, so what parcel is actually conveyed is not fixed by Section 1 alone. The tension is real but harmonisable.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause promises the balance "less any deductions identified below" and "or less dependent upon setoffs as described below", yet no deductions or setoffs are ever identified or described; it also runs a comma splice ("received by Buyer, For example") and gives a worked example that may or may not be a binding minimum. The interest sentence keys accrual to whether Detroit or Michigan pays interest "on the outstanding incurred eligible expenses", a phrase never defined.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The promised "below" deductions/setoffs appear nowhere — Section 28 merely repeats "less any setoff" without describing one, and Sections 9, 11 and 26 create other adjustments that may or may not be the intended deductions; the $9,000,000 total also has to be reconciled with the $8,000,000/$1,000,000 split and the contingent TIF stream. This is the provision most likely to have been construed.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It promises title "free from any and all liens or encumbrances" and in the same breath makes it subject to exceptions in an option agreement whose date is left blank, and "necessary to affect the Buyer's desired street closures" uses "affect" for "effect" while leaving "desired" undefined. The deed obligation is thus conditioned on a plat approval that may never issue.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 3 sources "Permitted Exceptions" from the Real Estate Option Agreement, while Section 4 speaks of "those Permitted Exceptions attached hereto" and the attachment list has "Exhibit B — Permitted Exceptions"; Section 8(a)(ii) adds "exceptions created or suffered by Buyer" as a further category. Those three sources of the same defined term do not obviously agree.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Seller ... shall have ten (10) business days prior to the date of Closing" is genuinely ambiguous as to when the cure window opens and closes, and the Title Company office and city are left blank; "sole cost and expanse" is a typo. Buyer's election must be made "prior to the expiration of the period for Seller to remedy", a period the clause never fixes with certainty.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It refers to Permitted Exceptions "attached hereto", which conflicts with Section 3's definition by reference to the Option Agreement, and its thirty-day delivery deadline sits against the ninety-day outside closing date in Section 8(a) without stating what happens if closing occurs sooner. The clash with Section 3 is specific.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "as a prepared in accordance with the 2005 ALTA standards" is garbled, and the clause fixes no delivery deadline and no consequence for non-delivery. Its subject matter — a survey reflecting a plat of vacation the City has not yet approved — makes the obligation contingent on an event outside either party's control.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It parallels Section 3's requirement of new legal descriptions from the same plat of vacation, and neither says what happens if the City never approves; Section 17's time-is-of-the-essence clause bites awkwardly on an obligation with no stated time. The mismatch is latent rather than a direct contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The "as is" acceptance of "all faults of every kind and nature whatsoever whether latent or patent and whether now or hereafter existing" is sweeping, but the carve-out "except as expressly set forth elsewhere in the Agreement" is attached only to the familiarity sentence, leaving its reach over the whole paragraph uncertain. That placement is exactly the sort of scope question a court construes.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It has to be reconciled with Section 7(d)-(e), where Seller gives affirmative environmental representations and warrants them true "on each day hereafter", and with Section 11, which puts risk of loss and repair on Seller until deed delivery — a blanket acceptance of hereafter-existing faults sits badly with both. That is a concrete, nameable tension.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: This is a bare introductory lead-in ("Seller covenants and represents to Buyer:") with no operative content of its own beyond blending "covenants" and "represents". There is almost nothing here to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its only fit issue is that the subparagraphs it introduces are variously absolute (7(a), 7(c)) and knowledge-qualified (7(b), 7(e)), while the closing sentence of Section 7 warrants them all absolutely. That belongs to those clauses, not to the lead-in.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short, definite representation of record ownership and corporate authority; no vague term and no list to construe. Standard and self-contained.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits comfortably with Section 3's deed obligation and Section 24's reference to the GSA Option, though the outstanding Option assigned to Buyer is an encumbrance on Seller's title that this representation does not address. No genuine contradiction found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "It has no knowledge of any teason" contains a scanning/typing error, and the representation mixes a knowledge qualifier ("to its knowledge") with an apparently absolute statement that "possession of the land has been peaceable and undisturbed". "Federal Office facilities contemplated herein" is a use never actually specified in this Agreement.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The "Federal Office facilities contemplated herein" hook depends on the Option Agreement and on Section 13's reference to "the contemplated use of the Property as a leasehold for Federal facilities"; and Section 7's closing sentence warrants this knowledge-qualified statement as absolutely "true and correct". The knowledge/absolute mismatch is a real internal wrinkle.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Of sufficient size, capacity" and "without any special charge, assessment or apparatus for its current use" are vague — sufficient for what, and what is "its current use" of a redevelopment site? The qualifier "for its current use" materially narrows an otherwise broad representation.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 26 repeats this representation almost verbatim but adds Gas, drops the words "for its current use", and then makes all utility terminations and relocations Buyer's sole cost — the two provisions cover the same ground with different scope. That is a specific, nameable inconsistency.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The disclosure that the property is a "facility" under MCL 324.20101 is definite, but "all environmental information that it has" is a soft, self-referential standard. Nothing else here is genuinely two-sided.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is expressly carved out of Section 7(e), and it sits against Section 6's blanket "as is" acceptance of environmental conditions and Section 7's closing continuing-truth warranty. The carve-out structure works, so the fit problem is modest.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "To the best of Seller's actual knowledge" qualifies three quite different representations, and subparagraph (3) is conditional on a hypothetical future purchaser availing itself of statutory exemptions, which makes the promise hard to apply. The stray dash in "(1) — that since Seller" is a mechanical artefact.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It excepts matters "indicated on Schedule A attached", but the Agreement's attachment list contains only Exhibit A (Legal Description) and Exhibit B (Permitted Exceptions) — there is no Schedule A anywhere in the instrument. It is also knowledge-qualified while Section 7's closing sentence warrants it absolutely and continuously.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Will continue to be true and correct on each day hereafter" is unbounded in time and unqualified, converting knowledge-limited representations into perpetual warranties. The absence of any "as of Closing" limit is a genuine construction question.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It directly overrides the knowledge qualifiers in 7(b) and 7(e) and interacts with Section 23's No Merger clause, which independently extends survival until acceptance of occupancy by GSA; the two survival regimes are not aligned. Naming Sections 7(e) and 23, the tension is specific.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The enumeration is broken — "(i) (ii) (iii) (iv)" appear as a bare run before any text, so the numbering of the closing obligations is corrupt on the face of the clause. "A mutually agreeable date" with a ninety-day backstop is otherwise workable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Closing is to occur at "the office of the Title Company", but Section 4 leaves the Title Company's office and city blank; the ninety-day outside date also has to be squared with Section 4's thirty-day title delivery and cure windows and with Section 17's time-of-the-essence rule. Those are real but manageable frictions.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Short and definite: deliver a recordable warranty deed subject to Permitted Exceptions. The only soft edge is "exceptions created or suffered by Buyer", where "suffered" is not defined.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It adds a category of permitted title exceptions that Section 3 does not contemplate, since Section 3 promises title "free from any and all liens or encumbrances" subject only to items in the Option Agreement. That is a narrow but nameable conflict with Section 3.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A standard FIRPTA transferor's certification with the defined terms supplied by Section 1445 of the Code; nothing vague. The trailing "such additional information as may be required thereunder" is anchored to the statute.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Nothing elsewhere in the Agreement touches foreign-person status; it does not interact with Sections 2, 8 or 9 in any troublesome way. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It is self-misnumbered — the text calls itself "Section 8(a)(v)" although it appears as (iv) and (v) is the possession clause — and "if required the Title Company" is missing a word. "Extraordinary obligations" is an undefined and genuinely elastic limit on an otherwise open-ended further-assurances duty.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The cross-reference error points at Section 8(a)(v) (Possession), and the clause overlaps Section 16's separate further-acts covenant, which contains no "extraordinary obligations" carve-out. The mislabelling is a concrete internal misfit.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: One sentence, unqualified: possession is delivered to Buyer at Closing. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It fits Section 8(a) and Section 11's transfer of risk on deed delivery; the only loose thread is Section 13's pre-closing entry rights, which are subject to Seller's existing uses. No genuine inconsistency.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "At the request of either party" makes escrow closing mandatory on unilateral demand, and "Title Policy" is capitalised though Section 4 uses "owner's title insurance policy" — small, but a defined-term slip. Cost sharing is clear at 50/50.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 4 places title-commitment costs at "Seller's sole cost", while this splits closing escrow fees and Title Company charges equally; the two cost allocations are close enough to argue about but not plainly contradictory. Checked against Sections 4 and 9.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "All real estate taxes, expenses and charges in connection with ownership and use of the Property" is a broad, unenumerated category whose reach is uncertain, and no proration convention or method is stated. That breadth is a modest but real vagueness.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 2 already describes "standard deductions and prorations (customary closing expenses incurred by the Seller inclusive of utility and real estate tax prorations)", and Section 26 makes utility relocation costs Buyer's alone; whether the Section 9 proration or the Section 2 deduction governs is not spelled out. That overlap with Section 2 is the concrete concern.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The Buyer-default limb is a tangle: "liquidated damages not to exceed $50,000" is followed by "In addition, the parties may seek any other remedy available at law or in equity", which is self-contradictory, and "fetter of credit" is a typo for "letter of credit". It is also unclear whether the letter of credit must be posted on execution or within ten business days of Award and Assignment, and "Any subsequent Buyer" is an undefined actor with no obvious referent.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The liquidated-damages cap has to be reconciled with Section 21's fee-shifting to the prevailing party and with Section 17's time-of-the-essence clause, and the five-day cure period sits against the ninety-day closing deadline in Section 8(a); the reversion of the $50,000 to Buyer on GSA revocation also depends on the Option referenced in Section 24. Multiple concrete points of friction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Injury beyond the ordinary wear and tear" and "an appropriate deduction from the purchase price" are both open-ended, and the choice between repairing and deducting is not allocated to either party. Whose election it is, and what "appropriate" means, is exactly the sort of thing litigated.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It squarely collides with Section 6, where Buyer accepts the Property "including all faults of every kind and nature whatsoever whether latent or patent and whether now or hereafter existing", and its price-deduction mechanism may be one of the unstated "deductions" promised "below" in Section 2. Both cross-references are specific.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The definition of a substantial taking — "such portion as would impair or otherwise affect the intended use of the Real Property" — is circular and extremely vague, since almost any taking "affects" use, and the first sentence ends in a period leaving a fragment before "Buyer shall have the right". "Real Property" is also a term the Agreement never defines, the defined term being "Property".
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The "intended use" hook depends on the federal-facility use described only in Sections 7(b), 13 and 23, and the ten-day notice window runs against the ninety-day closing framework in Section 8(a). The award allocation on termination (to Seller) is coherent with Section 1's award assignment language.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause is written in option-agreement vocabulary — "during the period of this Option including any extension periods", "Optionee", "Optionor" — none of which is defined in this purchase agreement, so it is not clear who owes the insurance, repair and notice duties. "Any other due diligence matters deemed reasonably prudent" is an unbounded catch-all following a specific list.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: This Agreement has no "Option period"; the Option is a separate instrument referenced in Sections 3 and 24, and Sections 8 and 17 fix the timetable by reference to execution and Closing, so the entry right's duration cannot be located within this document. That is a concrete whole-instrument misfit.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Three delivery methods are enumerated but the deemed-receipt sentence covers only mail and overnight courier, leaving personal delivery unaddressed — a classic expressio unius gap. The Buyer's notice address is simply blank.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The blank Buyer address undercuts every notice-dependent provision — Sections 4, 10 and 12 all turn on written notice and short deadlines — and the "copy to" party is GSA, whose consent Section 24 also requires for amendments. The gap is real though probably curable in practice.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Short and definite, though "payable to any other person or entity" reads oddly since neither party is a broker, and there is no indemnity attached. Little to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Nothing elsewhere in the Agreement deals with brokers or commissions; checked against Sections 2, 8 and 24 with no conflict. Fits cleanly.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Standard further-assurances language limited by "reasonably necessary"; that phrase is soft but conventional and courts apply it routinely. Nothing specific to name.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It duplicates Section 8(a)(iv)'s further-documentation duty, which carries an "extraordinary obligations" limitation that this clause lacks; whether that limit carries over is a small open question. Otherwise consistent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Clear and conventional, with an express weekend/holiday extension rule; "every provision hereof in which time is an element" is broad but determinate. Nothing genuinely ambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It bites hard on provisions that state no deadline at all (Section 5's survey, Section 3's plat-dependent deed) and on Section 4's oddly framed ten-business-day cure window, but strictness plus an open-ended obligation is a tension of application rather than a contradiction. Checked against Sections 4, 5 and 8.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Boilerplate headings clause, entirely conventional. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It fits the rest of the instrument without friction; checked against Sections 19 and 24. No conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Standard number-and-gender construction rule; short and unambiguous. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It coexists with Section 18's headings rule and Section 20's governing-law clause without difficulty. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "The laws of the state in which the Property is located" identifies Michigan indirectly but unmistakably; "permitted assigns" implies an assignment restriction the Agreement never states. That implication is a small loose end.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Agreement contemplates GSA involvement and an assigned federal Option (Sections 24 and 10), so a state-law-only choice sits awkwardly with a transaction whose other leg is a federal instrument, and "permitted assigns" has no anchor because no section governs assignment. The second point is specific.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Prevailing party, as determined by the court" is expressly delegated, and the recovery is limited to court costs and reasonable fees. Little room to argue.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It coexists with Section 10, whose $50,000 liquidated-damages cap and "any other remedy" language make it unclear whether fees sit inside or outside the cap. That interaction with Section 10 is the only real question.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Plain writing-and-signature requirement with a counterparts allowance; nothing vague within the clause itself. "Each party hereto" is definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 24 says the Agreement "may be amended only by written instrument, executed by the Buyer, Seller and the Government, acting by GSA" — that adds a third required signatory this clause omits, a direct conflict between Sections 22 and 24. Naming Section 24, the inconsistency is squarely on the page.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Survival is extended "until fulfilled, up to and including the time of completion of any improvements to be built thereon and the written acceptance of occupancy" — an end point tied to events this Agreement neither requires nor defines, and "until fulfilled" versus the occupancy date gives two different termini. That is genuine ambiguity in the survival period.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Nothing in the Agreement obliges anyone to build improvements or obtain GSA acceptance of occupancy — those come from the separate Option and lease procurement referenced in Sections 13 and 24 — and Section 7's closing sentence separately makes representations true "on each day hereafter". Two survival regimes that do not match.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause says the Agreement "cancels and supersedes all prior agreements" and "is entire in itself", then in the same sentence preserves the earlier Real Estate Option Agreement as an operative document — an integration clause at war with itself. The Option's date is also left blank ("dated , August, 2006") and the defined term is opened but never closed ("Option ).
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It requires GSA's signature for amendments while Section 22 requires only the parties' signatures, and it makes the Option operative alongside this Agreement without any order-of-precedence rule, even though Section 3 sources the Permitted Exceptions from that Option. Sections 22 and 3 are the concrete points of conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: One flat prohibition with no exceptions or remedy stated; nothing to construe on its face. The absence of a remedy is a gap, not an ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits against Section 8(a)(ii)'s "recordable Warranty Deed", but a bar on recording the contract is entirely compatible with recording the deed. No real conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "All public and quasi-public and private utilities terminations, and relocations" with "all costs associated therewith" is a sweeping, unenumerated cost allocation, and the stray "8" (a page number) has been absorbed into the sentence. "After closing" leaves pre-closing relocation costs unallocated.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It restates Section 7(c)'s utility representation but adds Gas and drops the qualifier "for its current use", and it then loads all relocation cost on Buyer despite 7(c) warranting availability "without any special charge, assessment or apparatus". That is a direct scope mismatch with Section 7(c).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Standard counterparts clause; the slight infelicity of "any one of which shall be considered an original" and "all of which ... one original" does not change meaning. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 22 separately permits amendments in counterparts; the two are consistent. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Will cooperate ... to secure all necessary government approvals" is an unmeasured best-efforts duty with no standard attached, and "any other applicable grant and/or loan programs" is an open catch-all after a specific reference to a Brownfield Plan. "Less any setoff" invokes a setoff regime the clause does not describe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its second sentence duplicates the last sentence of Section 2 but says "less any setoff" where Section 2 says "less any deductions" and promises setoffs "as described below" — this is the only later mention of setoff and it describes none, so the promised description is missing from the instrument. That circularity with Section 2 is the concrete defect.
